Other: concentrating solar power (CSP) systems prohibited; fenced array areas over 160 acres require a wildlife corridor; panels at least 24 in. above ground at maximum tilt.

description: Breckinridge County, Kentucky Ordinance 2025-0121 (Solar Energy Systems), second reading Feb. 17, 2025 (4-3), repealed and replaced Ordinance 2022-0321. Large-scale solar must be set back 1,000 ft from non-participating property lines and from public road and rail rights-of-way, and 2,000 ft from churches, schools, hospitals, residential buildings and incorporated city limits; the fiscal court may set more or less stringent setbacks case by case. In Clover Creek Solar Project LLC v. Breckinridge County Fiscal Court, the Kentucky Court of Appeals reversed the circuit court and held the ordinance invalid because the county has no planning and zoning commission under KRS Chapter 100; the county's motion for discretionary review is pending at the Kentucky Supreme Court.
long_description: setback: large-scale solar energy system footprint 1,000 ft from any non-participating property line and from the right-of-way of a publicly maintained road or rail line; 2,000 ft from any church, school, hospital, residential building or incorporated city limit; the fiscal court may require more or less stringent setbacks case by case. Also perimeter fencing and vegetative screening, a noise study, decommissioning within 12 months of ceasing generation with surety. Penalty $100 to $500 per day.

description: In October 2023, the Mohave County Board of Supervisors cast a 3-2 vote to establish a 240-day moratorium on using energy overlay re-zoning for the development of renewable energy on private property.
long_description: In October 2023, the Mohave County Board of Supervisors cast a 3-2 vote to establish a 240-day moratorium on using energy overlay re-zoning for the development of renewable energy on private property. In the four months prior to the moratorium’s adoption, the Board of Supervisors had denied every application for energy overlay re-zoning, including those for which the county’s planning and zoning commission recommended approval. Prior to the moratorium’s adoption, a local attorney opined that it would violate Arizona Statute 11-833, which limits moratoria on rural land to situations in which a county has demonstrated that a moratorium is necessary to “prevent irrevocable public harm” from a “clear and imminent danger.” In June 2024, the Mohave County Board of Supervisors voted 3-2 in favor of allowing solar projects within the county on land zoned for “Light Industrial” use, effectively lifting the prior moratorium.

description: In May 2023, the San Miguel County Board of Commissioners enacted a 6-month moratorium on applications for commercial energy projects (including solar projects), which was scheduled to expire in November 2024 after being extended twice.
long_description: In May 2023, the San Miguel County Board of Commissioners enacted a 6-month moratorium on applications for commercial energy projects (including solar projects), which was scheduled to expire in November 2024 after being extended twice. In September 2024, the Board unanimously adopted new zoning regulations on solar projects, ending the moratorium. The zoning regulations prioritize the siting of solar projects in areas that are already impacted by development. Large-scale solar projects of 30 acres or more are only permitted in certain districts and are not permitted in the Wright’s Mesa Light Industrial and Wright’s Mesa Rural Agricultural districts. Structures on solar farms are also required to be set back at least 200 feet from property lines.

The Council also decided against allowing wind turbines to make repairs affecting their height after the end of their contracts.

long_description: On September 24, 2024, Clinton County’s Planning and Zoning Commission issued a three-month moratorium on commercial wind farm applications as they revised the county’s 2008 wind ordinance. A community opposition group, Clinton & Jackson County Iowa Residents Against Wind Turbines, has collected over 700 signatures for a petition against the project and has been active in public hearings regarding the proposed ordinance. description: In August 2023, Twin Falls County Commissioners voted to institute a moratorium on large-scale energy projects on private land for 182 days.
long_description: In August 2023, Twin Falls County Commissioners voted to institute a moratorium on large-scale energy projects on private land for 182 days. The County defined “large scale” projects as those with a nameplate capacity of 10 MW or greater or requiring 100 or more acres of land. In March 2024, the Twin Falls County Commissioners unanimously passed a zoning ordinance regulating wind and solar energy projects. The ordinance prohibits new energy projects from being located on prime farmland, which it defines as farmland “which has the soil quality, growing season, and moisture supply needed to produce economically sustained high yields of crops when treated and managed according to acceptable farming methods.”

description: In 2017, Ford County imposed a moratorium on wind energy projects while it revised its ordinance.
long_description: In 2017, Ford County imposed a moratorium on wind energy projects while it revised its ordinance. In 2018, the county board’s zoning committee recommended increasing the existing 1,000-foot setback from buildings to 2,250 feet. At a hearing in October 2018, a group called Ford County Citizens for Property Rights demanded 3,250-foot setbacks from any property lines. On September 13, 2021, the County Board adopted an amended wind ordinance that increased setback to 2,250 feet from property lines upon which a primary structure is located. The ordinance further specified that, even if neighbors agreed to waive the setback requirement, any wind tower still must be at least 1,000 feet from the nearest primary structure. In 2023, Ford County amended its zoning rules to provide that, if the existing restrictions were “judicially determined to be invalid for any reason,” then the setbacks prescribed by Public Act 102-1123 (2023) would apply.

long_description: As of April 2019, twelve of the fifteen towns within Henry County had passed resolutions establishing buffer zones where no wind projects could be built. These buffers extend approximately 4 miles around each town. The twelve towns included Cadiz, Sulphur Springs, Kennard, Blountsville, Greensboro, Lewisville, Mount Summit, Springport, Straughn, and Middletown. In May 2019, Indiana passed a law limiting municipalities’ authority to enact such buffer zones going forward and voiding any such ordinances or resolution adopted after December 31, 2018. The law did not void any ordinances or resolutions adopted before January 1, 2019. Eleven of the Henry County town resolutions were grandfathered in under the law, but the town of Middletown’s was not.

description: The Woodson County Board of County Commissioners has enacted a moratorium and prohibition on Commercial Renewable Energy Projects in the unincorporated area of Woodson County.
long_description: The Woodson County Board of County Commissioners has enacted a moratorium and prohibition on Commercial Renewable Energy Projects in the unincorporated area of Woodson County. Specifically, the resolution directs the suspension of acting on any application for a Conditional Use Permit or permits for the erection and construction of any Commercial Renewable Energy Project (Section 1), prohibits the establishment of any such project (Section 3), and declares such establishment a violation of public interest while the resolution is in effect. No applications for Conditional Use permits shall be set for public hearing prior to 12 months from adoption (Section 2). The moratorium may be extended, terminated earlier, or amended by subsequent resolution (Section 5). The resolution “shall remain in effect until the end of February 2026” (Section 6). There are no stated conditions or exceptions limiting the prohibition to specific areas, prior approvals, or compliance status. The moratorium is currently in effect as of December 5, 2025.

On June 4, 2022, the Supreme Judicial Court struck down the restrictions, finding that “[a]n outright ban of large-scale solar energy systems in all but one to two percent of a municipality’s land area . . . restricts rather than promotes the legislative goal of promoting solar energy” and that, “in the absence of a reasonable basis grounded in public health, safety, or welfare, such a prohibition is impermissible.”  Note that this is included as a pre-March 2022 development because the relevant restriction was in place before March 2022.

long_description: In May 2023, Pelham residents voted to amend the town’s solar and energy storage bylaws. The town prohibited energy storage systems as a principal use in all zoning districts and required all large-scale solar projects (defined as installations between 1.5 and 15 acres of land) to be set back at least 500 feet from nearby streets. The town further required developers to set aside 4 times the total area of a solar installation for forestland conservation, if the project would convert any existing forestland for solar development. In December 2023, the Massachusetts Attorney General’s office sent a letter to the town rejecting portions of the amended bylaw, including the forestland conservation requirement, noting that certain bylaw provisions failed to comply with state law that prohibits municipalities from banning solar installations through zoning.

description: Shutesbury’s solar bylaw, adopted in May 2008 and amended in June 2021, prohibits solar plants larger than fifteen acres, among other restrictions.
long_description: Shutesbury’s solar bylaw, adopted in May 2008 and amended in June 2021, prohibits solar plants larger than fifteen acres, among other restrictions. In January 2023, Shutesbury residents voted to adopt a revised town bylaw for solar arrays at a Special Town Meeting. The revised bylaw would have banned energy storage systems as a principal use in all zoning districts and limited large-scale solar installations (defined as installations between 1.5 and 15 acres of land) to a special use in Forest Conservation Districts, prohibiting such installations in all other districts. The Massachusetts Attorney General’s office sent a letter to Shutesbury officials disapproving of the January 2023 bylaw, partially based on a determination that the bylaw violated state law by effectively banning solar installations. The Attorney General’s office’s action resulted in the pre-2023 bylaw regaining legal effect. The pre-2023 bylaw is the subject of a lawsuit filed by developer PureSky Energy in August 2023, in which PureSky alleges that the town’s solar regulations are in violation of state law that prohibits unreasonable regulation of solar energy systems.

long_description: On March 9, 2023, Carroll County adopted a 6-month moratorium on applications for community solar farms on land currently zoned for agricultural purposes. In December 2024, the Carroll County Board of Commissioners amended its land use ordinance to increase restrictions on commercial solar projects. Under the new ordinance, ground-mounted solar systems in residential and commercial districts cannot exceed 480 square feet, and projects must be set back at least 400 feet from any public transportation corridors. In addition, the height of ground-mounted systems cannot exceed 15 feet, and facilities must include a 12-foot-tall vegetative buffer along all property lines.

description: In November 2015, the Town of Freedom enacted a wind turbine ordinance that requires all wind turbines be set back 2,500 feet from any Scenic or Special Resource.
long_description: In November 2015, the Town of Freedom enacted a wind turbine ordinance that requires all wind turbines be set back 2,500 feet from any Scenic or Special Resource. Depending on the height and megawatt capacity of the turbine, the ordinance requires it be setback either 1.5 times turbine height, 3 times turbine height, or 13 times turbine height from non-participating landowners. Turbines less than 100 feet in height and less than or equal to 10 kW in capacity must be set back at least 1.5 times turbine height; turbines between 100 and 150 feet in height and less than or equal to 10 kW in capacity must be set back at least 3 times turbine height; and turbines greater than 150 feet in height and/or greater than 10 kW in capacity must be set back at least 13 times turbine height. The ordinance measures turbine height by the highest point of any turbine blade tip. Shadow flicker is limited to ten hours per year, and depending on the time of day and height of turbine, noise is limited to between 30 and 40 dBa.

As of October 2022, the township’s zoning ordinance requires that wind turbines be set back at least 1,760 feet from property lines or 4 times tower height, whichever is greater, and limits shadow flicker to zero; it also limits the height of commercial solar energy systems to 12 feet and requires that they be set back 500 feet from property lines.
source: Sabin Center, Opposition to Renewable Energy Facilities in the United States (June 2025 ed.), via data/renewable_opposition_records.csv

description: In April 2016, the Ellington Township Board of Trustees held a special meeting to vote on whether to enact a wind energy moratorium.
long_description: In April 2016, the Ellington Township Board of Trustees held a special meeting to vote on whether to enact a wind energy moratorium. By a unanimous vote, the board agreed to a 4-month moratorium on wind turbine development. The moratorium was supported by a group called Ellington-Almer Township Concerned Citizens, and it resulted in the delay of the Tuscola III wind farm.  The Ellington Township Zoning Ordinance, as amended July 2021, requires that wind turbines be set back by a distance of 5 times turbine height from property lines of non-participating parcels (i.e., 2,500 feet for a 500-foot turbine), and 3 times turbine height from any road. The ordinance further provides that noise shall not exceed 40 dBA at any time on a nonparticipating property and prohibits any shadow flicker on neighboring properties.

description: In May 2023, voters in Palmyra Township approved a zoning amendment that imposed new restrictions on utility-scale solar projects.
long_description: In May 2023, voters in Palmyra Township approved a zoning amendment that imposed new restrictions on utility-scale solar projects. While the original ordinance required that utility-scale solar projects be set back 50 feet from property lines, the amended ordinance requires setbacks of 330 feet. long_description: Sands Township disallows wind turbines in any zoning district—including agriculture and commercial districts—except for “Open Space” districts. Following the moratorium, the town amended its zoning laws to increase setbacks for solar projects: the town now requires 800-foot setbacks from county and state roads and 500-foot setbacks from all other roads.

description: On October 23, 2024, Wibaux County became the first county in Montana to adopt countywide zoning to restrict wind development.
long_description: On October 23, 2024, Wibaux County became the first county in Montana to adopt countywide zoning to restrict wind development. The rules were adopted as part of an effort to block AES’s proposal to construct the 235-MW Wibaux Wind Farm, which would include 50 MW of battery storage.

description: The Saline County Zoning Regulations, as amended in 2018, require that wind turbines be set back 0.5 miles from occupied structures on abutting properties.
long_description: The Saline County Zoning Regulations, as amended in 2018, require that wind turbines be set back 0.5 miles from occupied structures on abutting properties. The regulations further limit noise to 40 dBA for any 10-minute average at any dwelling. In August 2020, the Saline County Planning and Zoning Board approved a 4-month moratorium on new wind farm applications. After the 6-1 vote, the Board stated that the moratorium was meant to ensure community safety and the sustainable future development of wind energy in Saline County.

description: In September 2021, the Town of Vestal enacted a 6-month moratorium on approval of solar farms 25 kW or larger.
long_description: In September 2021, the Town of Vestal enacted a 6-month moratorium on approval of solar farms 25 kW or larger. In May 2022, the moratorium was extended by 1 year, and in May 2023, it was extended by another 6 months.  In June 2024, the Vestal Town Board unanimously voted to instate a 1-year moratorium on the approval of commercial solar farms, halting existing and future applications for solar farms. At public hearings on the moratorium, some residents expressed concerns about the potential negative impacts of solar farms, such as fire hazards and water contamination. In June 2025, the town adopted Local Law 4 to regulate Solar Energy Systems, effectively ending the moratorium. The law provides that commercial solar development is only allowed in the Commercial Development, Industrial, and Industrial Development Districts.

In February 2018, the Yates Town Board amended its wind energy facilities law to establish the following setback requirements: 3 miles from Lake Ontario; 1800 feet and 4.5 times total height from the boundary line of permitted wind development districts; 1800 feet and 4.5 total height from the Waterfront Revitalization Area Boundary; 2 times total height from non-residential structures; and the greater of 0.5 miles or 6 times total height from non-participant property lines, public roads, and highway rights-of-way, among other setback requirements.
source: Sabin Center, Opposition to Renewable Energy Facilities in the United States (Sept. 2026 ed.), via data/renewable_opposition_records_2026-09.csv
notes: Sabin 2026 entry 5711; rules: Setback Restriction (wind); county FIPS 36073

description: In November 2023, Mahoning County commissioners unanimously approved Green Township’s ban on large wind and solar projects in unincorporated parts of the township pursuant to S.B. 52.
jurisdiction: Green, Austintown, Beaver, Berlin, Canfield, Coitsville, Goshen, Jackson, Milton, Poland, and Springfield Townships
long_description: In November 2023, Mahoning County commissioners unanimously approved Green Township’s ban on large wind and solar projects in unincorporated parts of the township pursuant to S.B. 52. A public hearing was held in Green Township at the end of October 2023, in which residents were largely supportive of banning wind and solar. The ban had the effect of blocking the planned 150-MW Alpin Sun solar project. In February 2024, the Mahoning County Commission approved extending the ban to 10 additional townships within the county, namely: Austintown, Beaver, Berlin, Canfield, Coitsville, Goshen, Jackson, Milton, Poland, and Springfield.

long_description: In July 2024, the Smith Township Planning Commission began discussions to amend its solar and battery energy storage ordinance. long_description: In 2016, residents of Letcher Township in Sanborn County pre-emptively mobilized to block Juhl Energy from developing a wind project. Although Juhl Energy had not yet submitted an application, residents were concerned that the company would look to Letcher Township after nearby Davison County rejected its applicaion for a 9-to-11-turbine wind farm. In response to the petition, the Board of Supervisors voted to increase setbacks to 1 mile from dwellings of non-participating homeowners and 1,500 feet from property lines, making the project impossible to site.

description: In January 2015, the Northeastern Vermont Development Association (NVDA)—one of eleven Vermont regional planning commissions—unanimously approved a resolution against the development of all industrial wind energy systems.
jurisdiction: Caledonia County; Essex County; Orleans County
severity_basis: ban or moratorium (the source does not say which)
long_description: In January 2015, the Northeastern Vermont Development Association (NVDA)—one of eleven Vermont regional planning commissions—unanimously approved a resolution against the development of all industrial wind energy systems. The resolution states that “[i]t is the position of the NVDA that no further development of industrial-scale wind turbines should take place in the Northeast Kingdom.” This position was reaffirmed in NVDA’s 2018 Energy Plan and in NVDA’s June 2023 memorandum readopting that plan. NVDA’s resolution is not legally binding and is intended to serve as a “starting point” for member municipalities’ zoning process. These member municipalities are Caledonia, Essex, and Orleans counties.
source: Sabin Center, Opposition to Renewable Energy Facilities in the United States (Sept. 2026 ed.), via data/renewable_opposition_records_2026-09.csv
